chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, he said:
I asked him about the junub: may he recite the Qur'an? He said: up to seven verses. And in the narration of Zurʿah from Samāʿah, he said: seventy verses.

This report does not contradict the earlier reports in two ways. One of them is that we specify the earlier reports by means of this report, and say that their statement, peace be upon them: There is no problem in the two of them reciting whatever they wish from any place they wish, means up to seven verses or seventy verses.
And the second is that we interpret this report as indicating a kind of istihbab, not prohibition and obligation, while we interpret the earlier reports as indicating permissibility.
As for the obligatory surahs containing sajdah, it is not permissible for the two of them to recite them in any حالت; what indicates that is what...

key_terms.سَبْعِ آيَاتٍ: a limit of seven verses mentioned in the report
key_terms.سَبْعِينَ آيَةً: a limit of seventy verses mentioned in another version
key_terms.ٱلِاسْتِحْبَابِ: recommended practice rather than a binding rule
key_terms.ٱلْجُنُبِ: a person in the state of janabah requiring ghusl
key_terms.ٱلْعَزَائِمُ: the surahs or passages involving obligatory sajdah

ai.seo_question: Can a junub or ha'id recite the Qur'an, and are there limits on how many verses they may read?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the ruling on Qur'an recitation by the junub, and by extension the ha'id, presenting a report that limits recitation to a small number of verses. The text then reconciles this report with earlier narrations either by treating it as a specification of general permissibility or by understanding it as a recommendation rather than a binding restriction, while excluding the verses of obligatory sajdah from permissibility.
